title: Rewilding and the farmers next door

turns.speaker: Suki
turns.text: The estate's taking three thousand acres out of sheep and letting it go. Beavers in the river next spring.

turns.speaker: Callan
turns.text: The beaver part will be the fight. It always is.

turns.speaker: Eve
turns.text: For good reason, sometimes. They flood things. The difference is whether the people downstream were asked or told.

turns.speaker: Suki
turns.text: And the flooding is largely the point. A beaver wetland holds water back during heavy rain, so the town below floods less.

turns.speaker: Callan
turns.text: Which is a benefit to the town and a cost to the farmer whose bottom field is now a pond.

turns.speaker: Eve
turns.text: That's the whole thing in one sentence, really. Nobody's disputing the ecology. They're disputing who pays.

turns.speaker: Suki
turns.text: Payment for those services is meant to fix that, and it mostly hasn't arrived.

turns.speaker: Callan
turns.text: There's a cultural objection underneath it too, which gets dismissed as sentiment. Those hills have been grazed for eight hundred years. That landscape is also a human thing.

turns.speaker: Eve
turns.text: And rewilding tends to be bought by people from elsewhere, which doesn't help the argument.

turns.speaker: Suki
turns.text: No. Though the sheep economy up there survives on subsidy, so the choice isn't between wild land and a working farm.

turns.speaker: Callan
turns.text: That's true and nobody local likes hearing it.

turns.speaker: Eve
turns.text: It's the sort of fact that's correct and useless in a village hall.

turns.speaker: Suki
turns.text: Which is why the schemes that work start with the neighbours rather than the ecology.

points: An estate is taking three thousand acres out of sheep farming and reintroducing beavers.
Suki explains beaver wetlands hold back water during heavy rain, reducing flooding downstream.
Callan notes the benefit falls on the town while the cost falls on the farmer whose land floods.
Eve frames the dispute as being about who pays rather than about ecology, with payment for ecosystem services largely absent.
Callan raises a cultural objection, that centuries of grazing made the landscape a human creation, worsened by rewilding often being funded by outsiders.
Suki counters that upland sheep farming depends on subsidy, which Callan concedes is true but unwelcome locally.
